candidates.title: Forty Steps To Lunch
candidates.pitch: A visitor enters their lunch options and a few moods, then watches the candidates roll down a forty-station contraption where every station runs a real decision method: budget and distance gates, Condorcet and Kemeny voting, a simulated-annealing ember bed, a Monte Carlo robustness court, a Pareto gate and more. A vending machine drops the verdict, a receipt prints, and a leave-one-out audit names the few stations that actually changed the answer, while a shadow run shows what simply taking the first idea would have chosen. Stations can be added, reordered and tuned, and the long game is a machine in which all forty visibly do something.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless: lunch recurs daily, and the punchline is measured by the page instead of asserted. It also fills this week's owed humor slot with a working tool rather than a one-liner.

research.summary: The overengineering joke is an established genre with a clear lineage: dictionaries define the Rube Goldberg sense as complex means for a simple end, and a long-running Java repository satirises enterprise software by piling layers onto FizzBuzz. Lunch deciders are a familiar startup exercise, so the gag alone is thin. The depth comes from methods that are real and checkable: Condorcet cycles, the Condorcet family used in Debian leader votes, simulated annealing (named for metallurgy, introduced 1983) and expected value of perfect information as the ceiling on what extra deliberation can buy. The research shapes the mechanic: every station reports a measured effect, a leave-one-out audit finds the load-bearing stations, and an EVPI-style closing stage delivers the annoyingly correct verdict, measured by the page rather than claimed, of how often the extra deliberation changed anything.

facts.claim: Merriam-Webster defines the adjective Rube Goldberg as accomplishing by complex means what seemingly could be done simply, and the Britannica dictionary gives the same sense: doing something simple in an unnecessarily complicated way.
Pairwise majority voting over three or more options can produce a cycle (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A) even when every voter's own ranking is consistent; this is the Condorcet paradox.
Simulated annealing takes its name from annealing in metallurgy (heating, then controlled cooling) and is credited to Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi in 1983.

The expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the most that removing all uncertainty before deciding could be worth; it is never negative and is an upper bound on the value of any other information gathering.
As of the 2024 and 2025 vote pages, the Debian project uses the Condorcet method for its leader elections, and a LinuxFr report describes Debian's variant as the Schulze method.

FizzBuzz Enterprise Edition, a Java repository presented as satire of enterprise software, is a known example of piling layers onto a trivial task for comic effect, with much of the joke in its tongue-in-cheek issue tracker.
Commenters on a Hacker News thread about a lunch-picker site called building one a rite of passage for startups (reported, unconfirmed; one blended result).

design.coreLoop: The visitor sets the scene (options, budget, mood, weather), arranges stations on the conveyor, runs the machine, and watches candidate marbles pass each station while a ticker reports what that station measurably did. The receipt then shows the verdict, idle versus load-bearing stations from a leave-one-out audit, win frequency across thousands of perturbed worlds, and whether the first idea typed would have agreed. Tinkering continues toward two badges, all forty stations active and every active station load-bearing, and a shareable link replays the same machine.
sophisticationHooks: Forty-plus real stations in five families (gates, scorers, voters, stochastic searchers, consensus panels), each a pure function whose effect is measured as eliminations, rank movement or re-weighting, or reported as idle.
Leave-one-out ablation, Monte Carlo robustness and an EVPI-style closing stage produce the annoyingly correct verdict, including how often the naive first pick would have won anyway.
Order matters and is discoverable: a lottery before the filters wastes everything downstream, and a Pareto gate stays idle until a dominated option exists, which turns all-forty-active into a puzzle.

Presentation layer: SVG and canvas conveyor with anvil-drop eliminations, an ember-bed annealer, a vending-machine dispenser and a receipt with a hash-derived serial and barcode; machine, menu and daily seed live in the URL hash.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built in one morning: stage engine plus about 42 stations as small pure functions, an ablation and Monte Carlo worker, a conveyor renderer with a handful of station vignettes reused by family, vending machine and receipt, a drag-and-reorder editor with parameters, 24 hand-written lunch options with attributes, a date-seeded daily scenario, a templated copy module (three line variants per station, filled with real numbers), URL-hash state and an about panel. Cut: real restaurant data or maps, accounts, bespoke art per station, sound beyond optional synthesized clunks.
risks: Forty stations of real logic is the main scope risk; mitigated by building five family templates first, then parameterised variants, with a fallback of shipping thirty stations.
Copy volume across stations is large; templated lines filled with numbers from the actual run keep it from reading as canned.
A long animation can drag; skip and speed controls plus a static step list for reduced motion keep it quick.
Unverified: the 2015-era remark that lunch pickers are a startup rite of passage stays out of page copy, or appears as 'as of 2026-10-11, per a Hacker News comment'.
Close kin exist in enterprise-satire repositories; the differentiators are the measured-effect audit and the all-forty-active puzzle, and page copy has to lead with them.

Stage blurbs that cite method origins stay within verified facts (Condorcet cycles, the annealing name, the EVPI definition, Debian's Condorcet vote); other history is omitted. Lunch scores are the visitor's own ratings, labelled as entertainment, not advice.

candidates.title: Group Chat Gremlin
candidates.pitch: Five friends choose a movie with a real Raft-style protocol: they elect a Planner, replicate everyone's ballots into a shared log, and decide once three ballots are committed. The visitor plays the network, holding, dropping or reordering messages and crashing one friend within a mischief budget, while ember timers go dark, elections split and the minutes of the meeting write themselves. A live panel of Raft's safety properties stays green whatever the visitor does, so the game is stalling them, steering which movie wins through ballot order, or discovering that agreement is not fairness.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless: group chats still struggle to settle on a film, and the idea turns a real, teachable algorithm into a game. It fills this week's owed wildcard slot with a playable simulation rather than another explainer.

research.summary: Prose analogies that cast Raft as friends choosing lunch or dinner are already common, and interactive Raft visualisations exist, so a passive explainer would be a repeat. What the research supports as new is playing the adversary. The FLP result (1985) shows that with fully asynchronous delivery even one faulty process leaves every deterministic consensus protocol with a possible endless run, the Two Generals' Problem shows confirmations cannot remove doubt over lossy channels, and Raft answers with terms, majority votes and randomised election timeouts that make split votes unlikely, not impossible. Raft's five published safety properties give a live monitor that stays green whatever the visitor does, while ballot order decides which movie wins, which separates agreement from fairness. Lamport's Paxos paper was itself an allegory about a Greek parliament, which licenses the comic tone.

facts.claim: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson result (Journal of the ACM, 1985) shows that every deterministic protocol for asynchronous consensus has a possible non-terminating run even if just one process may fail, because a crashed process looks the same as a slow one.

In Raft a follower that hears no heartbeat within a randomised timeout (150-300 ms is the commonly cited example) becomes a candidate for a new term; a majority of votes wins, each term has at most one leader, and a split vote simply triggers another round.
The Raft paper lists five safety properties that hold at all times: Election Safety, Leader Append-Only, Log Matching, Leader Completeness and State Machine Safety.
Over a channel that can lose messages, no finite exchange of confirmations lets two parties be certain they agree (the Two Generals' Problem); extra messages only move the doubt to the last one.
Lamport's Paxos paper, The Part-Time Parliament, frames the protocol as the legislators of an ancient Greek island and appeared in ACM Transactions on Computer Systems in 1998.

Casting Raft as friends choosing dinner or lunch is already an established explainer genre (a DEV Community post, a database vendor's film-themed blog post, a conference talk on what to eat for lunch), so the new angle is making the visitor the adversary instead of the spectator.
An interactive Raft visualisation called The Secret Lives of Data exists (reported by a third-party software listing; unconfirmed, one blended result).

inspirations: The Secret Lives of Data (interactive Raft visualisation)

design.coreLoop: The visitor picks a level (stall them for twelve seconds, make a chosen movie win, or run the unlimited-mischief sandbox), reads the five friends' ember timers and ballots, then holds, drops or reorders messages and crashes one friend within a mischief budget while the protocol reacts in real time or in single steps. Each run ends with the verdict, a green safety panel, a fairness readout comparing the result with the all-five-ballots winner, and auto-written minutes of the meeting that double as a shareable replay link.
sophisticationHooks: A deterministic Raft core (terms, randomised election timeouts, vote requests with a log up-to-date check, append consistency check, majority commit, step-down on higher terms) run as a seeded discrete-event simulation that can be rewound, replayed and shared.
A live monitor of Raft's five safety properties that no attack can turn red, so every level is about liveness and fairness, not about breaking agreement.

The verdict is a state machine over the first three committed ballots, so delay-based ordering changes the winner and shows that consensus is not fairness; a regret readout compares against the all-ballots winner.

A mischief slider from none to unlimited: at unlimited, an attentive gremlin can keep them re-electing forever, a hands-on echo of the FLP result, while bounded budgets and randomised timeouts are what let them finish.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built in one morning: a Raft-lite engine with an event queue, an invariant monitor and a fuzz test over thousands of seeded random attacks; an SVG ring of five friends with travelling envelopes, ember timers and per-friend log strips; five levels plus a sandbox and a date-seeded daily challenge; a minutes-of-the-meeting generator with persona lines and callbacks; a hash-encoded seed and action list for replay; keyboard play with pause and single-step; an about panel. Cut: log compaction, membership changes, more than five nodes, real networking, music.
risks: The simplified Raft has to stay correct under every gremlin action; a seeded fuzz run with the invariant checker gates the build.
Newcomers may be lost; level one runs hands-off with plain-English envelope labels and a hover glossary.
Prior art: dinner-themed Raft explainers and passive visualisations exist, so page copy has to lead with the adversary game, outcome steering and the mischief slider.
Real-time play has to stay accessible: pause, single-step, full keyboard control and a message-list view for reduced motion.

FLP and Raft statements on the page stay within the verified facts; the 150-300 ms figure is shown as a commonly cited example, not a rule, and the unlimited-mischief mode is labelled as in the spirit of FLP, not a proof.

Unverified: that a named interactive Raft visualisation exists comes from a third-party listing; the page names it only as 'as of 2026-10-11, per a software listing' or omits it. Friends and movie titles are invented; no real films, brands or people.
